metadata.title: NLRB v. Town & Country Elec., Inc., 516 U.S. 85 (1995) (No. 94-947)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: NLRB v. Town & Country Elec., Inc.

Opinion filed: 1995-11-28

Docket No.: 94-947

Citations:
• 133 L. Ed. 2d 371
• 116 S. Ct. 450
• 516 U.S. 85
• 1995 U.S. LEXIS 8311

Case holding summaries:
• discussing salting activities of unions and holding that salts are "employees" as defined in the National Labor Relations Act, 29 U.S.C. § 152(3)
• stating “[s]ince the task of defining the term ‘employee’ is one that has been assigned primarily to the agency created by Congress to administer the Act, . . . the Board’s construction of that term is entitled to considerable deference”
• "[U]nion organizing, when done for pay but during nonwork hours, would seem equivalent to simple moonlighting, a practice wholly consistent with a company's control over its workers as to their assigned duties."
• using common-law test to distinguish between "employee" and "independent contractor" under Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, 29 U. S. C. § 1001 et seq.
• Congress delegated to the Board "primary responsibility for developing and applying national labor policy"
• employer restrictions on union solicitation during nonworking time in nonworking areas are presumptively invalid under the Act
• some confidential workers, although "employees," may be excluded from bargaining unit
• using common-law test to distinguish between "employee" and "independent contractor" under NLRA
• certain "confidential employees" fall within the definition of "employees"
• retired persons are not "employees" because they do not "work for another for hire"
• the Board's views are entitled to "the greatest deference"
• worker who was intoxicated while on duty, "came to work when he chose and . . . left the plant and his shift as he pleased," and utterly failed to perform his assigned duties is still an "employee" protected under the Act
• arsonist who is also union member is still an "employee," but may be discharged
• paid union organizers can be "employees" protected by the Act
• independent contractorlike newsboys are "employees"
• statutory word "employee" includes job applicants, for otherwise the Act's prohibition of "`discrimination in regard to hire' " would "serve no function"
• interpretations of the Board, the agency that Congress "`created . .. to administer the Act,' " will be upheld if "reasonably defensible"
• using common-law test to distinguish between "employee" and "independent contractor" under Copyright Act of 1976, 17 U. S. C. § 101 et seq.
• holding that “the Board often possesses a degree of legal leeway when it interprets its governing statute, particularly where Congress likely intended an understanding of labor relations to guide the Act’s application”
• worker can be servant of union and employee of company at same time
• observing that we afford “a degree of legal leeway” to Board interpretations of NLRA
• “[The Supreme Court’s] decisions recognize that the [NLRB] often possesses a degree of legal leeway when it interprets its governing statute, particularly where Congress likely intended an understanding of labor relations to guide the [NLRA]’s application.”
• a company worker that is simultaneously a paid union organizer fits the statutory definition of employee
• discussing broad construction of the term "employee"
• "A company faced with unlawful (or possibly unlawful) activity can discipline or dismiss the worker, file a complaint with the Board, or notify law enforcement authorities."
• not- ing that, while paid union organizers are employees protected by the Act, the Board has held that they "may not share a sufficient ‘commu- nity of interest’ with other employees (as to wages, hours, and work- ing conditions) to warrant inclusion in the same bargaining unit"
• ruling that union salts are protected as “employees” under the NLRA
• holding paid salts are protected as “employees” under the NLRA
